newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK land supply tight, unequal to demand - Tsang.
newsitem.headline: HK land supply tight, unequal to demand - Tsang.

text.p: Hong Kong Financial Secretary Donald Tsang acknowledged on Thursday that the territory's land supply is tight and not adequate to match rising demand, and is a factor in high property prices.

"In terms of property prices, it's a consequence of market movements. We have seen our demand rising and that demand had not been matched by adequate land supply," Tsang told a morning radio show on the 1997/98 budget after he presented it on Wednesday.
"I do appreciate that for last year and for this year the supply still continues to be tight."
Tsang said it was a matter the government would address.
"We, of course, have been trying to do our best. In the budget speech, I mentioned that we are going to supply a lot more in the coming five years than the previous five years," he said.
In his budget speech, Tsang said the government plans to release 46 percent more land for residential development over the next five years than it had over the past five years.
Property prices have been on the rise since last year, particularly towards the end of 1996. The government has blamed the increases on speculation and threatened to take steps against it.
Tsang reiterated that the administration was monitoring the situation and would take measures if speculation got out of hand.
"If there are any signs of speculation getting rampant again, I am sure more measures will be introduced," Tsang said.

In January, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, the territory's de facto central bank, recommended that the maximum loan-to-value ratio for high-end properties with a value of more than HK$12 million be reduced to 60 percent from 70 percent.

But Tsang said the administration would be cautious over the implementation of anti-speculation measures as they could also have a negative impact on the market, as was the case in 1994 when the government launched such measures.

"We introduced a whole series of measures to stamp out our speculator activities. The result was, yes, we drove them out of the market. But they have brought into the market a certain disadvantage," he said.

"For instance, our developers had just been redeveloping for a long while, hence we are seeing a shortage of supply at the moment. So there we have to be rather cautious on what we are going to do," he said.
The previous anti-speculation measures led to a property market slump that saw prices fall 10-30 percent from 1994 peaks.
Tsang also warned developers against setting prices at excessively high levels.

"At the moment they have a good run. But they have to be rather careful in that when prices reach a certain level which is not sustainable by underlying rents then of course it means ...the red signal will be blinking again," Tsang said.
